source.title: BLOCK-NORMALIZED GRADIENT METHOD: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY FOR TRAINING DEEP NEURAL NETWORK
source.authors: Adams Wei Yu; Lei Huang; Qihang Lin; R. Salakhutdinov; J. Carbonell

record.tranche_reason: The study compares held-out performance of Adam and momentum SGD on image-classification tasks, bearing on the optimizer comparison in V4; its main intervention is block-wise gradient normalization.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's direct Adam-versus-SGDM test-error comparisons. The normalized-gradient variants are not extracted because they are a different optimizer intervention. The paper also reports optimizer comparisons on PTB and Rotten Tomatoes, but those results do not provide the Adam-versus-SGDM comparison needed for V4.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares Adam and momentum SGD on held-out image-classification and language-task performance. Its baseline comparisons test V4 despite its main focus on gradient normalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that block-wise gradient normalization improves optimization and often held-out performance, especially in deep networks. They describe SGDM as uniformly better than Adam on CIFAR ResNets, but their plain-optimizer table entries contradict that description for CIFAR10 ResNet-56 and -110 and CIFAR100 ResNet-110. They also report SGDM outperforming Adam on ImageNet and Adam outperforming SGDM on sentiment classification.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates block-wise gradient normalization and compares it with unnormalized optimizer baselines; the Adam-versus-SGDM comparisons use the study's stated experimental setups, not a test of the original optimizer-generalization studies' full tuning protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Adam-versus-SGDM ordering varies by dataset and model depth: it reverses for CIFAR100 ResNet-110. The paper states that normalized-gradient methods with constant step size perform better on deep CNNs, while adaptive step-size methods perform better on RNNs.
record.problems: CIFAR residual-network comparisons report means and variances, but the ImageNet comparison is one experiment with no uncertainty stated. The study does not report the broader tuning conditions in V4.
record.rows_left_out: No Adam-versus-SGDM comparison is provided in the PTB or Rotten Tomatoes results, so those optimizer results were not extracted for V4. The paper's many block-normalized and clipping variant results were left out because they are not the optimizer comparison named by V4.

untested.parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Controlled convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.

Broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and whether worse held-out performance occurs despite equal or better training performance. The supplied text does not resolve the plain Adam-versus-SGDM ordering in the PTB curves.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout interventions; PTB uses dropout throughout without a no-dropout control.

missing.what: The claimed omission rationale is incorrect: Table 4 directly compares plain Adam (74.02%) with plain SGDM (64.35%) on best validation accuracy. Add this V4 comparison despite its mistaken exclusion in rows_left_out.

record.verdict_notes: The main extraction error is confusing SGDM with SGDMNG in the last two CIFAR10 columns. CIFAR uncertainties are described by the authors as variances; their precise interpretation is unclear. PTB and MNIST figures include plain optimizer comparisons, but the supplied text preserves no readable curve ordering sufficient for additional verdicts. This study is not an original source of V4.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
Width sweeps past interpolation are not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures are not compared.
The study does not compare broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, or word-level language-model Adam against SGD.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets are not tested.
Dropout effects on held-out error are not tested.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps are not measured.
Removing memorized examples and retraining are not tested.
